Stop and reconsider the roots of cyberpunk. In the 20th century, guys like Cordwainer Smith and Sam Delaney were writing about cyborgs. New Wave sci-fi adopted some cyborg stories, and New Wave sci-fi was all about the 1970s hedonism and its desire to rebel against the dominant Christian ethos of the West. So of course New Wave glorified sex, drugs, and perversion rather than wholesome heroes and exploration of unknown planets. Cyberpunk stories often glorify hedonism, but simultaneously warn that hedonism has undesirable after-effects and unforeseen consequences.

Cyberpunk fiction has its roots in body horror. In the 1980s, nobody was talking about "transhumanism" as such, but people were finally getting simultaneously grossed out and fascinated by the technologies that later got labeled as transhumanism. People were thinking about cyborg bodies and saying, "Hey, even if this were not ethically questionable, it's just stomach-churningly nauseating." Cyborgs were seen as part of "body horror" writing in the 1980s. (Check out books like Dr. Adder and When Gravity Fails to see that authors can be fascinated by transhumanist surgical alterations without endorsing it as desirable.)
